stories.headline: Ukraine says it sank a Russian warship in Libya as the war spreads beyond the front
stories.summary: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine was behind naval drone attacks that sank a Russian warship and damaged a sanctioned cargo vessel in Libya, thousands of miles from the front line. Ukraine called the strikes lawful self-defense. Zelenskyy has also confirmed a drone strike on a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland, while Poland reported a Russian drone in its airspace days after Russian missiles landed on its territory.
stories.why_it_matters: The fighting between Russia and Ukraine is now reaching the Mediterranean, the Baltic and NATO territory, which raises the chance of other countries being drawn in and of disruption to shipping routes.
stories.background: Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and the war is now in its fifth year. Ukraine has used explosive-laden sea drones to hit Russian ships in the Black Sea, and reporting earlier this year said Ukrainian forces were operating in Libya and had attacked a Russian tanker in the Mediterranean. Libya is split between rival administrations in Tripoli in the west and in the east, where Russia has a military presence and where Benghazi is located. Russia continues nightly air attacks on Ukrainian cities.

facts.text: Zelenskyy said Ukraine carried out attacks that sank a Russian warship and damaged a sanctioned cargo vessel in Libya.
Zelenskyy posted military video said to show the naval drone attacks.
Fox News identified the ship as the corvette Mercury and the location as Benghazi.

Ukraine said the strikes were lawful self-defense; the Kyiv Independent quoted an official, Tykhyi, as saying Russian warships and arms carriers arriving in Libya were what created a threat to the country.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Ukrainian special forces tracked Russian ship movements for months before the attack.
Zelenskyy confirmed Ukraine was responsible for a drone strike on a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland, Bloomberg reported.

Poland said a Russian drone entered its airspace during an overnight attack on western Ukraine, days after three Russian missiles came down in Poland; an air-attack alert was issued for parts of the Lublin region for about an hour.
The Kremlin has not commented on the missiles that landed in Poland, NPR reported.
A Russian attack on the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia overnight killed two people, regional governor Mykhailo Semikin said.

The Financial Times, citing people familiar with the matter, reported that U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has not yet approved the transfer of about 60 Patriot interceptors already allocated to Ukraine.

stories.headline: COP31 climate summit ends without a deal after split over fossil fuels
stories.summary: The United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, ended without an agreement after the European Union and other parties refused to accept a final text that lacked language on phasing out fossil fuels. The EU now plans to seek changes to how the UN talks are run, the Financial Times reported.
stories.why_it_matters: These yearly talks are where governments set shared goals for cutting emissions and paying for climate damage; a failed summit means no new global commitments this year, and experts quoted by the AP say poorer countries could be hit hardest.
stories.background: COP is the annual UN conference where nearly every country negotiates climate action, and decisions require consensus. This year's meeting, COP31, was held in Antalya, Turkey. An early draft called for faster action to phase out fossil fuels, but a later, shorter draft removed that language as the deadline approached. Countries were also divided over climate finance, the money richer nations provide to help poorer ones cut emissions and cope with climate impacts.

facts.text: COP31 ended without an agreement, with divisions over fossil fuels and climate finance.

About 130 parties, including the EU and Panama, refused to accept the COP president's consensus text, saying it "greenwashes" fossil fuels; India, China and Saudi Arabia were on the other side, The Hindu reported.
A slimmed-down draft published before the Friday deadline had removed any reference to ending the use of fossil fuels.
The EU will seek changes to the UN climate talks process after the failure, the Financial Times reported.
Experts told the AP that the failed talks could worsen climate inequality, though not all progress has stalled.
France 24 reported disappointment among African countries with the outcome.

stories.headline: Ousted Bangladeshi leader Sheikh Hasina sets Dec. 16 return; government vows arrest
stories.summary: Former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina plans to return to Bangladesh from exile in India on Dec. 16, her spokesperson said. Bangladeshi officials said she would be arrested if she comes back and that they expect India to honor the two countries' extradition treaty.
stories.why_it_matters: Hasina was sentenced to death in absentia, and her planned return is already fueling political tension and street violence in Bangladesh, according to The Hindu.
stories.background: Sheikh Hasina ruled Bangladesh for 15 years until a student-led uprising forced her out on Aug. 5, 2024, when she went to India. She was sentenced to death in absentia last year over a crackdown on protesters that left hundreds dead. She has said several times that she wants to go back, but had not named a date before. Dec. 16 is the anniversary of the end of Bangladesh's 1971 liberation war with Pakistan.

facts.text: Hasina's spokesperson said she plans to return to Bangladesh from India on Dec. 16.
It is the first time she has set a date for her return, the BBC reported.
The spokesperson told Reuters she seeks to travel on the state carrier.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said Hasina would be arrested on return and that Dhaka expects India to honor the extradition treaty.
Another official, Humaiun Kobir, said she could only be brought back "in handcuffs or under strict surveillance."
Bangladesh's law minister said earlier that she would be arrested on arrival, before she could surrender to a court.

stories.headline: UK sanctions Myanmar generals after genocide ruling; Malaysia to keep sending people back
stories.summary: Fourteen countries formally acknowledged the International Court of Justice's finding that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, and the United Kingdom sanctioned top Myanmar military leaders. Malaysia's prime minister said his country will repatriate another 6,803 Myanmar nationals next month despite the ruling.
stories.why_it_matters: It is the first time the UN's top court has found a state responsible for genocide, and how governments respond will shape what such rulings mean in practice, including for Rohingya refugees.
stories.background: The Rohingya are a mostly Muslim minority from Myanmar; military operations in 2016-2017 drove large numbers of them into Bangladesh. Gambia brought a case against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice in 2019 under the Genocide Convention. On Nov. 19 the court ruled 9-6 that Myanmar committed genocide and said Gambia could seek reparations for victims, with amounts to be set later. Myanmar has been run by a military junta since a 2021 coup and is fighting a civil war.

facts.text: Fourteen countries from Europe, Africa and Oceania acknowledged the ICJ ruling and called on Myanmar to comply with its obligations under international law.
The UK imposed sanctions on top Myanmar military leaders after the ruling.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Malaysia plans to repatriate another 6,803 Myanmar nationals next month.
Anwar said Malaysia would continue working with Myanmar on repatriation and acknowledged "atrocities" by the junta.
The ICJ ruled by nine votes to six that Myanmar committed genocide, the first time the court has found a state responsible for genocide, according to Human Rights Watch.
A report released Tuesday by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines said land mine casualties hit a five-year high in 2025, with Myanmar's civil war a main driver.

stories.headline: Mexico says captured drug lord 'El Chapo Isidro' will be tried at home; U.S. drone aided raid
stories.summary: Mexican officials said the United States flew a surveillance drone over Mexican territory to help locate Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as 'El Chapo Isidro', who was captured in a special forces raid in Sinaloa. A Mexican official said he will be tried in Mexico despite a U.S. extradition request.
stories.why_it_matters: The case shows how far U.S. involvement in Mexico's fight against cartels now extends and tests whether arresting leaders reduces the flow of drugs and violence, something analysts cited by Reuters say has a mixed record.
stories.background: Meza Flores is an alleged trafficker based in Sinaloa state who was on the FBI's most-wanted list and had avoided capture for years. The United States has pressed Mexico to act against cartels and has sought the extradition of their leaders. Mexico has recently detained several senior cartel figures. U.S. military or intelligence activity on Mexican soil is politically sensitive in Mexico.

facts.text: Mexican officials said the U.S. flew a surveillance drone over Mexican territory to help locate and capture Meza Flores.
He was captured in Sinaloa in a special forces raid coordinated with U.S. intelligence, and the capture led to further arrests.
A Mexican official said he will be tried in Mexico despite a U.S. extradition request.
Authorities released body-camera footage of troops detaining him at a home.

stories.headline: NATO pledges space defense after reports Russia may launch a nuclear-armed satellite
stories.summary: German media, citing unnamed German military and intelligence sources, reported that Russia may be preparing to launch a satellite carrying a nuclear weapon. Asked about the reports, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance would defend against threats in space. The reports have not been confirmed on the record.
stories.why_it_matters: A nuclear blast in orbit could disable satellites that phones, navigation, banking and weather forecasting depend on, but the claim rests on unnamed sources.
stories.background: Western officials have said since at least 2025 that Russia may be developing a nuclear device meant to destroy satellites. Rutte said in 2025 that such a weapon would breach the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bars nuclear weapons in orbit. The new reports come from German outlets citing the military and the BND, Germany's foreign intelligence service. Tension between Russia and NATO is already high over the war in Ukraine.

facts.text: German media, citing unnamed German military and BND sources, reported that Russia may be preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite in the coming weeks.
Rutte said Monday that NATO would defend against threats in space.
The reports said such a weapon would give Russia the ability to destroy other satellites.
Rutte said in April 2025 that putting nuclear weapons in space would violate the 1967 Outer Space Treaty.

stories.headline: Israel's likely next leader says Iran is no immediate threat, clashing with Netanyahu
stories.summary: Gadi Eisenkot, who has the mandate to form Israel's next government, said he sees no immediate threat from Iran that requires military action. Caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned against playing down what he called grave threats. Separately, the U.S. ambassador to Israel said he was not certain American military aid would end this year, as President Donald Trump had promised.
stories.why_it_matters: Whether Israel strikes Iran again affects the risk of a wider Middle East war and oil prices, and the dispute over U.S. aid involves $3.8 billion a year in American taxpayer money.
stories.background: Israel held an election on Oct. 27, and President Isaac Herzog then asked Eisenkot, a former army chief, to form a government instead of Netanyahu, who stays on as caretaker prime minister during coalition talks. Netanyahu has pushed for renewed strikes on Iran, and Fox News reports that Trump is weighing them. The United States gives Israel $3.8 billion a year in military aid. Trump said on the day of this month's U.S. midterm elections that the aid would end by the end of this year.

facts.text: Eisenkot said he sees no immediate threat from Iran requiring military action.
Netanyahu warned against playing down "grave threats."
Herzog tasked Eisenkot with forming a government after 67 lawmakers endorsed him; Netanyahu remains prime minister in a caretaker capacity.
U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee said he was "not certain" the $3.8 billion in annual U.S. military aid to Israel would end this year, as Trump promised.
Israeli political leaders, among them a rival of Netanyahu, condemned what they called "Jewish terrorism" after settler attacks on Palestinian villages in the West Bank over the weekend.

stories.headline: Iran flogs singer and four colleagues over concert performed without hijab, lawyers say
stories.summary: Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi and four members of her team each received 74 lashes in the city of Qom, according to their lawyers and an Iranian news website. They were also banned from artistic work and travel for two years.
stories.why_it_matters: The case shows that Iran is carrying out corporal punishment against women and artists who defy its dress and performance rules, which Western governments and rights groups call torture.
stories.background: Iranian law requires women to cover their hair in public and restricts women from singing solo in public. Ahmadi posted an online concert in December 2024 in which she performed without a headscarf. A court in Qom sentenced her and members of her team in June to 74 lashes each, plus two-year bans on travel and artistic activity. Flogging is a legal punishment in Iran.

facts.text: Ahmadi and four others, described as three musicians and a producer, each received 74 lashes in Qom, according to their lawyers.
Reuters attributed the report to the Iranian website Emtedad, which quoted lawyer Mostafa Nili.
The five were also given two-year bans on artistic and musical activity and travel.
The sentence was for offending public decency through the content they produced and published, the Guardian reported.
Western governments and rights groups have criticized flogging as torture and a violation of international law.
The sentence was reported in June 2026 and stems from an online concert filmed in December 2024.
